Central Nervous System
Physiology
Pyramidal, Extrapyramidal tracts

Quick Overview

This lesson covers the descending tracts, the pathways through which upper motor neurons control the lower motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle. They are split into the pyramidal system (corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticonuclear tracts), which initiates skilled voluntary movement, and the extrapyramidal system (reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, rubrospinal, olivospinal and tectospinal tracts), which regulates tone, posture and gross movements. For each tract the lesson gives its origin, course, crossing pattern and function.

Descending Tracts and the Control of Movement

Steps in producing a voluntary movement

Accurate voluntary movement requires cooperation between many higher and lower nerve centers:

  1. The order of the movement is developed in the motor association areas of the frontal lobe.
  2. The program and pattern of the movement are developed in the basal ganglia and cerebellum, which modulate and modify muscle performance according to afferent impulses from the muscles.
  3. Motor area 4 and premotor area 6 send the excitatory impulses to the skeletal muscles that carry out the movement.

Two types of skeletal muscle contraction

  • Reflex contraction (e.g. the withdrawal reflex): needs only intact lower motor neurons (LMN). These lie in the anterior horn cells (AHC) of the spinal cord for limb and trunk muscles, and in the brain stem for head and neck muscles. Their axons form the motor nerves to skeletal muscle.
  • Voluntary contraction (e.g. writing, skilled movements): needs intact LMN and upper motor neurons (UMN), which are found in the motor and premotor areas of the cerebral cortex and in other brain stem centers.

UMN damage: voluntary movement is lost, but reflex movements can still occur.

LMN damage: both voluntary and reflex movements are lost, even if the UMN are intact.

Role of the descending tracts

The activity of the LMN (both alpha and gamma cells) is controlled by the UMN through a group of fibers collectively called the descending tracts. These tracts control voluntary movements, muscle tone and even autonomic functions, enabling skeletal muscles to perform their proper functions. They reach the alpha and gamma cells of the anterior horn either directly or through multisynaptic pathways.

The descending tracts are classified into two groups: pyramidal tracts and extrapyramidal tracts.

Pyramidal Tracts

General features

  • A one-way, direct connection between the UMN and the AHC.
  • Contains about one million fibers, of which only 60% are myelinated; myelination is complete one year after birth.
  • Called "pyramidal" because it is the only tract containing axons of the Betz (pyramidal) cells, found in the 5th layer of motor area 4 and in no other area.
  • Betz-cell axons form only 5% of the tract; the origin and functions of the unmyelinated fibers are still not exactly known.

Parts of the pyramidal tracts

TractOriginTerminationKey points
Corticospinal 30% area 4; 30% premotor area 6; 40% somatic sensory areas (3, 1, 2 and 5, 7) Interneurons and AHC at different spinal levels Crossed (lateral), direct (ventral) and ipsilateral components
Corticobulbar Mainly lower parts of areas 4 and 6 Motor nuclei of cranial nerves V, VII, IX, X, XI and XII Partly crossed, partly uncrossed (bilateral innervation)
Corticonuclear Frontal eye field, area 8 Nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV and VI (extraocular muscles) of both sides Reaches the nuclei via the medial longitudinal bundle

Course of the corticospinal tract

  1. Cerebral cortex: the axons form the corona radiata and occupy the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
  2. Midbrain: the fibers are grouped in bundles and form 3/5 of the basis pedunculi.
  3. Pons: the fibers descend in the basis pontis.
  4. Medulla oblongata: the fibers form the elevations called the pyramids, where they divide as below.

Fate of the fibers in the medulla

  • 80% cross to the opposite side (motor decussation) and descend in the cord as the lateral corticospinal tract, ending around interneurons and AHC at different levels.
  • About 20% descend on the same side as the direct (ventral) corticospinal tract, but re-cross to the opposite side at different cervical and thoracic levels to end around the AHC.
  • Only 1% descends without crossing as the ipsilateral corticospinal tract, supplying AHC of the same side.

Corticobulbar and corticonuclear tracts

The corticobulbar tract supplies the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves that innervate muscles and glands of the head and neck. A large part of its fibers cross in the brain stem, but many innervate the same side. The corticonuclear tract arises from the frontal eye field (area 8) and supplies the nuclei of both sides; it produces conjugate deviation of both eyes to the opposite side and accommodation to near and far vision.

Double innervation: because the cranial nerve nuclei are supplied from both sides, the face is little affected in an internal capsule lesion.

Exceptions: the whole hypoglossal nucleus and the lower half of the facial nucleus are innervated only from the opposite pyramidal tract.

Functions of the pyramidal tract

  1. Initiates and facilitates isolated skilled voluntary movements, especially those needing training and education, such as writing, threading a needle and typing.
  2. Increases muscle tone and other deep reflexes.
  3. Inhibits the primitive withdrawal reflex (Babinski's sign).

Extrapyramidal Tracts

General features

  • Any descending tract other than the pyramidal; they are "multi-station" fibers arising from wider areas: cortical areas 4 and 6, the basal ganglia, and brain stem centers (reticular formation, tectum of the midbrain, red nucleus, olivary nuclei, vestibular nucleus).
  • Extrapyramidal fibers from the premotor area mix with pyramidal fibers in the corona radiata and internal capsule (anterior limb) before reaching the basal ganglia.
  • Some tracts descend directly without crossing, others cross, and a third type innervates both sides.
  • The brain stem centers receive impulses from the premotor area, basal ganglia, cerebellum and motor area, and their activity is largely controlled by these connections.
  • The tracts terminate around the gamma cells (mainly) and alpha cells of the AHC at different spinal levels.

The main extrapyramidal tracts

TractOriginCourseFunction
Medial reticulospinal Pontine reticular formation Descends directly, without crossing Facilitatory to muscle tone
Lateral reticulospinal Medullary reticular formation Crosses to the opposite side Inhibitory to muscle tone
Vestibulospinal (lateral and medial) Vestibular nuclei Descends without crossing; ends on AHC at different spinal levels Facilitates tone, especially of extensors (antigravity muscles); carries the pathways of postural reflexes arising from the labyrinth
Rubrospinal Red nucleus of the midbrain, which receives impulses from higher cortical areas, basal ganglia and cerebellum Crosses rapidly in the midbrain to the opposite side Mainly inhibitory to tone; controls many muscle activities through the "cortico-rubro-spinal system"
Olivospinal Inferior olivary nuclei of the medulla, which receive impulses from the basal ganglia Descends without crossing; a relatively short tract ending around AHC only as far as the cervical region Facilitatory to muscle tone
Tectospinal Lateral: superior colliculus. Medial: inferior colliculus (midbrain) Crosses to the opposite side; ends around AHC of the cervical region, which control neck muscle movements and movements such as raising the arms in front of the eyes Coordinates visual and auditory spinal protective reflexes, e.g. reflex turning of the head away from or towards visual or auditory stimuli

Functions of the extrapyramidal system

  1. Helps the pyramidal tract in coordinating isolated skilled muscle movements; alone it cannot initiate them. A pure extrapyramidal lesion causes no paralysis but great disturbance of muscle movements.
  2. Alone, it can coordinate gross involuntary movements of the big joints, which need bulky proximal muscle groups.
  3. Regulates muscle tone (some tracts are excitatory, others inhibitory).
  4. Maintains equilibrium and adjusts body posture.
  5. Controls visceral functions through descending tracts:
    • Respiratory tracts: from the respiratory centers to the AHC of the respiratory muscles.
    • Vasomotor tract: from the vasomotor center to the lateral horn cells in the thoracic and lumbar region.
    • Vesicomotor tract: controls abdominal and pelvic floor muscles during micturition.
    • Sweat secretion tract: from the heat-regulating center in the hypothalamus to the lateral horn cells in the thoraco-lumbar region.

Key Points / Quick Review

Motor control basics

  • Movement order: motor association areas; program: basal ganglia and cerebellum; execution: areas 4 and 6.
  • UMN lesion: voluntary movement lost, reflexes preserved.
  • LMN lesion: voluntary and reflex movements both lost.

Pyramidal tract identity

  • Direct UMN-to-AHC pathway; about 1 million fibers, 60% myelinated.
  • Contains Betz-cell axons (layer 5 of area 4), only 5% of the tract.
  • Origin (corticospinal): 30% area 4, 30% area 6, 40% areas 3, 1, 2 and 5, 7.

Corticospinal course

  • Corona radiata, then anterior 2/3 of the posterior limb of the internal capsule, then 3/5 of basis pedunculi, then basis pontis, then medullary pyramids.
  • 80% cross (lateral tract); about 20% direct tract that re-crosses; 1% ipsilateral.

Corticobulbar and corticonuclear

  • Corticobulbar: cranial nuclei V, VII, IX, X, XI, XII; largely bilateral.
  • Hypoglossal nucleus and lower half of the facial nucleus: opposite side only.
  • Corticonuclear (area 8): nuclei III, IV, VI of both sides; conjugate deviation of the eyes to the opposite side.

Pyramidal functions

  • Initiates skilled voluntary movements.
  • Increases muscle tone and deep reflexes.
  • Inhibits the primitive withdrawal reflex (Babinski's sign).

Extrapyramidal tracts and tone

  • Facilitatory: medial reticulospinal (pontine), vestibulospinal, olivospinal.
  • Inhibitory: lateral reticulospinal (medullary), rubrospinal.
  • Rubrospinal and tectospinal cross; medial reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and olivospinal do not.
  • Tectospinal: visual and auditory protective reflexes of the head and neck.

Extrapyramidal functions

  • Assists skilled movements but cannot initiate them; lesions cause disturbed movement, not paralysis.
  • Coordinates gross involuntary movements, tone, equilibrium and posture.
  • Controls respiratory, vasomotor, vesicomotor and sweat secretion functions.
